One shelf, one proper fallback meal. Unexpected guests are easier to feed when one cupboard can produce a complete, flexible meal. This kit makes tomato-and-white-bean pasta, with optional olives and a simple fruit finish. It starts with shelf-stable ingredients and uses one pasta pot, one saucepan and a colander. Plan on four adult main-meal portions. Appetites differ, so keep an extra packet of pasta and another can of beans if your usual group needs more. The assembly is designed for roughly twenty-five minutes; hob strength and the pasta's cooking time will decide the actual finish. The message to send firstYou're very welcome. I'm planning pasta with tomato sauce and white beans, with toppings separate. Any allergies or food needs I should check before I start? Show the actual ingredient labels if needed. A shelf-stable kit is a hosting shortcut, not a promise that every ingredient suits every guest. The exact four-person kit. 12 ounces / 340 grams dry pasta: short shapes are easy to portion. Keep the packet's cooking directions.1 jar, approximately 24 ounces / 680 grams, tomato pasta sauce: choose a flavor your household already enjoys.2 cans, approximately 15 ounces / 425 grams each, cooked white beans: cannellini or navy beans, drained and rinsed before serving.1 tablespoon olive oil: optional, for the finished dish.½ teaspoon dried oregano: optional; leave it out if the sauce is already well seasoned.½ cup pitted olives: optional, served separately with their own spoon.4 sealed fruit cups, approximately 4 ounces / 113 grams each: or one approximately 20-ounce / 567-gram can of fruit, divided four ways.Water and salt: use the pasta packet's water guidance; salt is optional and can be adjusted at the table. For two, use half the pasta and sauce, one bean can and two fruit cups. Refrigerate opened ingredients according to their labels. For six, multiply by one and a half: 18 ounces pasta, 36 ounces sauce, three bean cans and six fruit cups. Use a pot big enough for the larger quantity. Store this group in one ordinary box or beside each other on a shelf. Keep a manual can opener nearby. Put a note on the box: “Four-person pasta meal. Replace anything borrowed.” No special storage bins required. A twenty-five-minute assembly plan. Minutes 0–3: check and set up. Confirm the guest's food needs, read labels and wash hands. Fill the pasta pot as directed on its packet and bring it to a boil. Set out four bowls and a colander. Clean can lids before opening.Minutes 3–7: build the sauce. Drain and rinse the beans. Put the tomato sauce, beans and optional oregano in the saucepan. Heat gently, stirring so the bottom does not catch. Add 2–4 tablespoons water if it is very thick. Follow any heating instructions on the sauce and bean labels.Minutes 7–18: cook the pasta. Once the water boils, add the pasta and set a timer for its package cooking time. Stir. Keep the sauce at a gentle simmer while the pasta cooks, stirring occasionally. Put olives in a separate dish and set out the fruit.Minutes 18–22: check and combine. Test pasta for the texture wanted. Before draining, carefully reserve ½ cup cooking water. Drain. Combine with the sauce, or keep them separate if preferred. Add reserved water a tablespoon at a time if the sauce needs loosening.Minutes 22–25: serve. Divide into four bowls. Add olive oil if using, then offer toppings separately. If the pasta needs longer, follow its directions; there is no prize for meeting the timer. For someone who prefers unmixed foods, reserve their plain pasta before combining. Keep a familiar backup available if the person wants it. They do not need to try a new sauce to join the meal. Useful substitutions, without a second shopping trip. No white beans: use two same-size cans of chickpeas. The texture will be firmer. Keep them separate if that suits the group.No jarred sauce: combine one 28-ounce / 794-gram can of crushed tomatoes, 1 tablespoon olive oil and ½ teaspoon dried oregano. Simmer gently for 10–15 minutes while the pasta cooks; season to taste. It will be less rich than many prepared sauces.No pasta: use four portions of shelf-stable, ready-to-heat rice prepared exactly as its packet directs. Spoon the bean sauce over it. Do not assume a particular pouch is ready to eat cold.Gluten-free requirement: choose appropriately labeled pasta and check the sauce and toppings. Use clean equipment and discuss cross-contact needs with the guest.More people than food: cook extra pasta and open extra beans in the same proportions. A can of vegetables served separately can add another side; four portions do not become six just by changing bowls. Ten-minute, no-hob alternative for four: only if the products are labeled ready to eat, drain and rinse the two cans of beans, then toss with 2 tablespoons olive oil and 1 tablespoon vinegar. Offer approximately 8 ounces / 225 grams of crackers, the olives and fruit alongside. This is a lighter meal. Check ingredients and each person's usual texture requirements. Keep the shortcut food-safe. “Shelf-stable” applies to suitable unopened products. Anything labeled “Keep Refrigerated” belongs in the fridge, including some canned foods. Check the USDA's explanation of shelf-stable food. Do not use leaking, bulging or badly dented cans, or jars with compromised lids. Do not taste suspect food to check it. The USDA's canned-food guidance explains warning signs and storage. Serve promptly. If holding food, keep hot food at 140°F / 60°C or above and cold food at 40°F / 4°C or below. Refrigerate perishables within two hours, or one hour above 90°F / 32°C. Discard food that exceeds those limits. Divide leftovers into shallow containers for prompt chilling. These are the FDA's buffet-safety rules. Allergies need a direct conversation, original labels and suitable preparation. Keeping toppings separate does not by itself prevent cross-contact. Communication · AAC · Access Communication is an ecosystem, not a device. Speech, an AAC app, a look toward the door, a sign, a photograph, a typed sentence, a switch, a sound, a paper board or an established yes/no signal can all be part of one person’s communication. The goal is not to force one “best” mode. It is to make enough reliable routes available that the person can say what they mean, where they are, with the body and energy they have that day. One visual route is useful. A whole communication system includes the person, their access method, their language, their partners, and a backup when the first route is not workable. No prerequisitesASHA guidance says AAC should not be withheld because of age or presumed cognitive, language or motor prerequisites. More than requestingA full system needs room for refusal, opinions, jokes, questions, repair, social closeness and sharing information—not only “I want.” Always availableCommunication tools should stay accessible across settings, including low-tech backups when electronics are impractical. Evidence and links checked October 2, 2026. This is practical family guidance, not an individualized AAC evaluation. In this guideWhat countsHow a person accesses languageCommunication partnersReal-life examplesAI + emerging techAuthorship + evidencePrintable profile 01 / Multimodal by design Use every reliable route. Do not make speech the tollbooth. ASHA describes AAC as inherently multimodal: a person may combine speech or vocalizations with gestures, signs, facial expression, objects, pictures, photographs, writing, spelling, communication boards, text-to-speech and speech-generating devices. The mix can change by place, communication partner, motor access, fatigue, sensory load and message. AaSpeech + vocalizationWords, approximations, sounds, intonation, laughter and other intentional vocal signals. ✋Gesture + signPointing, reaching, conventional gestures, manual signs, body orientation and established movements. ▦Symbols + picturesPhotographs, visual scenes, communication books, symbol grids and meaningful objects. ⌨Writing + spellingHandwriting, typing, texting, alphabet boards and text-to-speech when independently accessed. ◉Eye gaze + scanningDirect eye-gaze selection, switches, auditory or visual scanning, and partner-assisted scanning. ▣Speech-generating techDedicated devices, tablets or phones with robust symbol- or text-based language systems. A useful distinction: message vs. route“I need a break” is the message. Speech, pressing a symbol, looking to a “break” card, signing, pointing to the door or selecting “yes” during partner-assisted scanning are possible routes. When one route becomes hard, the message still deserves another route. Behavior can carry information. It is not a mind-reading system. A change in movement, pacing, vocalization or facial expression may tell a familiar partner that something is different. Respond to the person and the situation, but do not assign a precise message without a way to confirm it. “You seem uncomfortable. Is something wrong?” plus an accessible way to answer protects agency better than deciding what the behavior “means.” Visual example: a tiny backup board This is deliberately small: it is the sort of emergency board that might live in a pool bag or glove compartment. It is not a substitute for a person’s full vocabulary. YESNOSTOPBREAKHELPMOREFINISHEDSOMETHING ELSE ASHA’s 2026 AAC Awareness Month materials specifically highlight public communication boards as useful low-tech access in places such as libraries and parks. A public board is an additional route—not a reason to leave someone’s personal AAC behind. 02 / Access is part of language The same vocabulary can be reached in very different ways. Touch is only one access method. ASHA describes direct selection through touch, joystick, eye gaze, head mouse, trackball or other signals, and indirect selection through scanning. In partner-assisted scanning, the partner presents choices in an agreed sequence and the communicator makes the selection with an established independent signal such as a look, blink, movement, sound or switch. Direct touchUseful when target size, motor planning and positioning make touch reliable. Do not shrink buttons simply to fit more vocabulary. Eye gazeCan be low-tech with an eye-gaze frame or high-tech with a camera-based system. Calibration, positioning, lighting and visual access matter. Switch + scanningItems are highlighted or spoken in sequence; the user activates a switch or signal when the desired item appears. Partner-assisted scanningLow-tech and powerful when the person has a dependable selection signal. The partner presents; the communicator selects. Keyboard / textTyping can be paired with word prediction, stored phrases or text-to-speech to reduce effort while preserving authorship. Multiple access methodsA person may touch at a table, use partner-assisted scanning in a pool, and use eye gaze when motor fatigue makes direct touch unreliable. Access changes. That does not mean the person has “lost” communication.Before deciding a system is not working, check positioning, target size, sensory conditions, fatigue, vision, hearing, device volume, charging, vocabulary location, partner familiarity and whether the person has a lower-effort alternative. Screen time is not the right frame for communication. ASHA explicitly notes that concerns about ordinary recreational screen time do not apply to screens used as part of an AAC system. A communication device is access to language. 03 / Partner skill The people around AAC are part of the system too. A sophisticated device with rushed or controlling partners can still produce very little real communication. Communication-partner instruction has a research base, and common strategies include aided modeling, expectant delay, responsive interaction and practice across everyday settings. Model, do not quiz.Use the person’s AAC while you talk, especially for words beyond requesting. Show language without demanding imitation. Wait longer than feels natural.Looking, navigating, motor planning and composing a message can take time. Do not fill every silence. Respond to every credible attempt.A gesture, device selection, word, look or sign deserves a response even when the answer to the request is no. Talk to the person.Ask the AAC user the question. A support person can help with access without becoming the person being addressed. Leave room for “no.”A communication system that can only produce compliance is not a full communication system. Repair together.Try “I think I missed that. Can we try another way?” rather than pretending to understand. Model a wide range of reasons to communicate. refuseaskcommentjoketell newscomplainflirtask for helpsay “not that”talk about painchange the subjectend the conversation Presume a right to communicate, not a message you have already decided.Respecting competence means offering meaningful language, access and time. It does not mean claiming to know what someone intended before they have a reliable way to indicate it. 04 / In ordinary life Build redundancy before the hard moment. A multimodal plan is most useful when it answers a simple question: What can this person use here, right now, if their usual route is difficult? PoolElectronics and water do not mix.Keep the primary device available in a safe dry place, and add a waterproof or laminated board for words such as stop, more, out, bathroom, cold, help, finished and something else. Decide how yes/no will work in the water. RestaurantMenus create extra language demands.Use the person’s robust AAC, a photo or actual menu, pointing, text, or a short choice display. Keep “none of these,” “something else,” “not hungry,” and comments available—not only food requests. School / programConsistency matters more than identical behavior.Keep the same core language available across rooms and staff. A printed backup, charging plan, access instructions and a short communication passport reduce the risk that AAC disappears when one adult is absent. Medical visitDo not let the historian replace the patient.Ask the person first when possible. Prepare vocabulary for location, intensity, yes/no/not sure, body parts, fear, stop, explain again and “I need a break.” A familiar supporter can clarify access and history without answering everything by default. High stressLanguage may need a lower-effort route.Keep a small, predictable set for urgent messages—stop, break, help, pain, bathroom, home, not that, yes/no—while preserving access to the full system when the person wants it. With unfamiliar peopleMake the rules visible.A one-sentence note can say: “Please speak directly to me, wait for my answer, and do not move my communication system without asking.” Before leaving the house Primary AAC or established communication tools are charged, mounted or packed. A low-tech backup can cover yes, no, stop, help, break, finished and something else. At least one adult knows the person’s reliable yes/no and selection signals. Vocabulary for this setting has been added without removing access to the rest of the language system. The person can refuse, change the subject and end an activity—not only request it. There is a plan for water, battery, Wi-Fi failure, glare, noise or a device that suddenly stops cooperating. Copy checklistReset 05 / What is genuinely new AI can reduce effort. It should not become the author. Current AAC research is exploring smarter prediction, personalized vocabulary, expressive synthetic speech, emotion-related features and new access methods. The useful test is not “does it look futuristic?” but “does it increase speed, independence, precision or participation without taking control of the message?” Useful nowPrediction + stored languageWord prediction, phrase prediction and well-chosen stored messages can reduce keystrokes. A 2025 AAC study explored partner-suggested vocabulary in a dual-tablet system as a way to increase efficiency. Suggestions should remain suggestions: the communicator accepts, rejects or changes them. EmergingAI-assisted expressionA 2026 preliminary study explored AI-based emotion recognition as one possible AAC feature. Interesting is not the same as settled. An algorithm’s guess about emotion should never be treated as the person’s statement of how they feel. Research frontierBrain-computer interfacesBCI research is advancing for people with severe motor impairment, including communication applications. 2026 reviews describe promise but also major variability, usability, training and ethics questions. It remains an emerging access route, not a general replacement for established AAC. Privacy deserves a place in the setup. AAC can contain extremely personal language: health information, relationships, location, private conversations and custom vocabulary. When a system adds cloud prediction or AI features, check what is uploaded, stored, used for model improvement, synced across devices or visible to support staff. Convenience should not quietly erase communication privacy. A good AI rule for AACAI may help find, predict, pronounce or organize a message. It should not decide the person’s meaning. Keep the final selection under the communicator’s control and make generated suggestions easy to reject. 06 / Authorship matters Support access without confusing the supporter with the author. Some communication methods involve another person, so the key question is who is selecting the message. Partner-assisted scanning can preserve authorship when the partner presents options and the communicator makes each selection using an established independent signal. Letterboards are not all the same thing. A letterboard or alphabet board can be ordinary low-tech AAC when the person independently points, looks or otherwise selects letters. That is different from methods in which a facilitator physically guides, steadies or cues the person in a way that may determine the selection. What major professional guidance saysASHA identifies Facilitated Communication (FC) as discredited and says it should not be used because controlled research has shown facilitator authorship. ASHA also does not recommend Rapid Prompting Method (RPM), including Spelling to Communicate (S2C), because of prompt-dependency and lack of scientific validity; messages produced through these methods should not simply be assumed to be authored by the disabled person. That concern is about authorship and evidence—not about denying nonspeaking people access to spelling, literacy or robust AAC. Questions that protect authorship Can the person make the selection without another person touching or directing their hand, arm or board? Is the person’s selection signal defined and observable? Can unfamiliar or differently positioned partners obtain the same kind of response? Can the person disagree with the partner, choose unexpected vocabulary and initiate a topic? If the message has serious consequences, is there a way to verify authorship without leading the answer? 07 / Copy + print A one-page multimodal communication profile Keep this practical. It should help an unfamiliar person communicate better in the next ten minutes—not summarize someone’s life. My communication routes People should speak to me by… I may communicate using… My reliable YES is… My reliable NO is… Please give me about… If my primary method is hard, try… Important words for today… Please do NOT… Copy profilePrint profileClear One more line worth adding“If you are not sure what I meant, please tell me. Give me another way to try.” Communication repair is a skill shared by both people in the conversation. Sources + further reading Where this guide is grounded. Start with a real interest. Swimming, music, food, a favorite film, being outside: an activity has a better starting point when there is something the person enjoys in it. Ask in the way they communicate, allow time, and pay attention to their response. Familiar preferences can help you offer possibilities without deciding everything for them. Keep the choices real. If there is time for either a short walk or a visit to the pool, offer those. A long list of unavailable activities makes the decision harder for everyone. Show the actual item or place when that is useful.Break a large choice into smaller ones: activity first, then time or what to bring.Include a way to say “no,” “something else,” “break” or “finished.”Use the person's established communication methods and usual support. Age-respectful does not mean policing someone's taste. A much-loved character, toy or familiar activity can remain a genuine favorite. Present choices respectfully and let the person enjoy what they enjoy. Find a part worth taking part in. Look at an everyday activity and separate the pieces. For assembling a gift, someone could choose the item, select the paper, place it in a bag or decide which ribbon to use. For an outing, they could choose the destination or the music for the journey. Prepare the parts that would otherwise get in the way, using the support the person ordinarily has. Keep their chosen role meaningful. If they select the blue paper, use the blue paper. Their contribution should affect what happens. Before you begin Put the materials within comfortable reach and keep the workspace clear.Explain or show what is happening in a familiar way.Check whether the tools, closures and instructions are manageable with the usual assistance.Leave enough time for a response before adding another instruction.Make a pause or an early finish possible. A first try can be brief. Watching, choosing, doing one part or returning another day are all possible ways to join in. Offer assistance without making independence the price of participation, and let a refusal remain a refusal. Shop for access in the details. Before buying an activity or product, trace the steps between opening it and enjoying it. Does it require reading, precise timing, several tiny pieces or repeated setup? Can it be restarted easily? Is the enjoyable part accessible with the support already available? Clothes, accessories and everyday equipment Consider the wearer's preferred look alongside fabric, fit and fastenings. For a bag or device accessory, check actual dimensions, weight, access to controls and how it will be carried. A long feature list tells you very little about an awkward zip. Plans outside the house Ask about group size, noise, waiting, facilities and whether the usual support person can join. Find out what a shorter visit would involve and where a break can happen. A clear description or a few current photographs may help make the plan familiar. Keep personal information private when arranging support. Share the access details the host needs, and discuss photos separately rather than assuming participation includes being photographed. Afterward, consider what the teen seemed to enjoy and ask for their view in an accessible way. Keep the useful parts and adjust the awkward ones. A good activity leaves room for both help and personal choice.

Older-teen life · SwimmingA better swim outing for an older teenThe best swim plan is age-respectful, practical and built around the person who is actually getting in the water — not around what an activity is ‘supposed’ to look like. In this guideArrivalThe bagParticipationThe exit Check the arrival before the water. Find out where to enter, whether there is a line, what the changing area is like and where a support person may go. Ask about family or accessible changing rooms when those are useful, and confirm the rules for support people before arriving. Pack for comfort, not performance. Bring the swimwear that already works, a familiar towel or robe, dry clothes, easy shoes, water, the person’s communication, and the ordinary support items they use. A new outing is usually not the day to test six new products. Let the water be the activity. Swimming laps, walking in the water, floating, sitting on the steps or staying for twenty minutes can all count as a real swim outing. Start with what the person enjoys and build support around that. Make leaving easy. Decide where dry clothes go, what the quick exit looks like and whether food or another preferred stop comes next. The transition out of the pool often deserves as much planning as getting in. Keep goingRelated guidesOlder-teen editPool packing kitQuiet-break plan

Wardrobe · Family lifeThe low-drama photo-day planA good photograph does not require a brand-new personality, a complicated outfit or an hour of styling. Make the familiar version look a little more intentional and protect the routine around it. In this guideThe outfitFive-minute groomingBackupNo perfection Choose comfort first. Start with a shirt, sweater or dress shape the person already tolerates. Then choose the cleanest, best-fitting version in a color that works with the background. Avoid testing scratchy collars, stiff shoes or complicated fastenings on the same morning. Do the visible things only. Prioritize clean face, tidy hair, comfortable clothes and one quick check for lint or food marks. Stop before the preparation becomes harder than the picture. Bring one backup. A second familiar top can solve a spill or last-minute refusal without turning the morning into a wardrobe debate. Keep it simple and easy to change into. Let the photograph be enough. Not every person looks at the camera or smiles on cue. A photograph can still be excellent when it looks like the person who was actually there. Profoundly AwesomeMake room for the whole person.High support needs are part of everyday family life here. So are preferences, humor, privacy, favorite places and the pleasure of a day that works.In this guideKeep the person in the conversation.Plan one good thing, with space around it.Let dignity shape the small decisions. Keep the person in the conversation. We use “profound autism” to describe our family's particular experience of very high support needs. The term is contested, and it is not everyone's preferred language. This is one family's perspective. Individual autistic people and families have their own experiences and ways of describing them. In everyday company, start by speaking to the person you are with. Make room for the communication methods they use and the time they need. Their usual support can be part of the conversation without the conversation passing them by. Ask about an actual preference, such as where to sit or what to do next.Keep familiar communication tools available and ask before touching them.Avoid piling several questions together or answering immediately on the person's behalf.Use a tone that respects their age, including when the words need to be straightforward. A person may need extensive help throughout the day. Their preferences still belong in the plan, including when they want to pause, decline or change direction.Read our detailed guide to multimodal communication, AAC, access methods and communication-partner support → Plan one good thing, with space around it. A swim, a familiar lunch, time outside or a favorite shop can be enough for a day out. Choose the part that matters most, then check the practical details that make it possible: arrival, waiting, food, bathrooms, breaks and the way home. Describe the plan in a familiar format. Actual photographs, objects, words or the person's established communication system may be useful. Include what comes afterward and how a change of plan will be explained. Keep a shorter version ready. Think through what happens if the visit is brief. Can you leave and return? Is there somewhere comfortable to pause? Can one family member finish an activity while another leaves with their support person? Agree on the practical arrangements before everyone is tired. Bring the everyday supplies and communication equipment the person ordinarily uses, and follow their existing support plans. Where possible, distribute the packing, transport and checking among the people available to help. Afterward, ask what worked and notice what the person chose to return to. Repeating a familiar pleasure is a perfectly good plan. A family day does not need a new destination every time. Let dignity shape the small decisions. Privacy matters at home, with friends and online. A difficult moment, personal care or an intimate detail can stay private. Before sharing a story or photograph, consider whose experience it is, what the person has communicated about it, and whether the detail needs to be public at all. Leave it out when permission is unclear. A useful handover can be brief. For an activity host or someone helping with the day, share the practical information they need: how the person communicates, what support helps them take part, how to offer a break and whom to contact if plans change. Keep private care information with the appropriate people through a suitable private channel. A simple starting point is: “Please speak directly to them and allow time to respond. They communicate using [method]. For this activity, [specific support] helps. If they want to pause, [familiar signal or arrangement].” Adapt it to the person and the setting. The useful questions remain ordinary ones. Did they have a say? Could they join in with the help they needed? Was there room to stop? Were their private moments protected? Those details make everyday life more considerate for the person at its center.
